intro: Sydney's oldest trees are colonial garden plantings, and two of the most famous are not the original tree at all. The Camperdown Cemetery fig went in the year the cemetery opened, 1848. The Bidwill kauri in the Royal Botanic Garden grew from seed collected on New Year's Day 1849 by the Garden's first director. The jacaranda in the university Quadrangle and the Botanic Garden's Wishing Tree are both replacements for celebrated predecessors that died, which their pages say in the first line rather than the last.
meta_description: Sydney's remarkable trees: an 1848 Moreton Bay fig in Camperdown Cemetery, the Bidwill kauri grown from 1849 seed, and two honest replacements.
question_answer: Sydney's oldest documented tree is the Moreton Bay fig in Camperdown Cemetery in Newtown, planted in 1848, the year the cemetery itself opened, with a canopy now spanning more than thirty metres. The Bidwill Kauri in the Royal Botanic Garden runs it close: its seed was collected at Maryborough in Queensland on New Year's Day 1849 and the tree was planted in 1853.
question_meta: The Moreton Bay fig in Camperdown Cemetery, planted in 1848 when the cemetery opened, is Sydney's oldest documented tree.
question_context: Sydney is a young city for trees and an honest answer says so. Everything datable here was planted by colonists in the middle of the nineteenth century, which puts the oldest at not quite two hundred years, and the trees that people talk about most are younger still. The jacaranda in the University of Sydney Quadrangle is famous enough to appear in graduation photographs and superstition, and the tree standing there today is a clone planted in 2017 after the 1928 original died the year before. The Botanic Garden's Wishing Tree carries a plaque saying outright that it will never match the tree it replaced, a Norfolk Island pine from around 1816 that died in 1945. Neither belongs on a list of old trees under any other description, and both are here because the place itself is worth standing in. The genuinely old ones are the figs. Camperdown Cemetery's dates from 1848, Vaucluse House's Port Jackson fig from the 1850s, and a fig on a Woolwich verge was dated to about 1900 by a council officer reading old photographs.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Sydney?
faq.a: The Moreton Bay fig in Camperdown Cemetery, Newtown, planted in 1848 when the cemetery opened. Its canopy now spans more than thirty metres.

faq.q: Is the Quadrangle jacaranda the original one?
faq.a: No. The 1928 tree died in 2016 and was replaced in 2017 by a clone grown from its own material, so the tree standing there now is about nine years old. The university kept the same spot and the same genetics.

faq.q: Where can I see several of Sydney's trees in one go?
faq.a: The Royal Botanic Garden holds two, the Bidwill Kauri in the Palm Grove and the Wishing Tree towards the harbour side. The rest are spread out: Newtown, Camperdown, Vaucluse and Woolwich are separate trips.

Not all of them. Four of the six pins are approximate, meaning we know the garden, cemetery or street but not the trunk, and the pages say which. If you find one, tell us where it stands and we will sharpen the pin.

trees.name: The Bidwill Kauri Pine

location.address: Palm Grove, Royal Botanic Garden Sydney, Mrs Macquaries Road, Sydney NSW 2000

trees.access: Free; Royal Botanic Garden Sydney, open daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Martin Place or St James stations
trees.notes: Pin: OpenStreetMap carries an unnamed Agathis robusta node at this point in the Palm Grove, the only one of that species mapped inside the Garden, which is a better spot than the Garden's centre the first pass used. One crowd-maintained source and no name on the node, so the precision stays approximate.
trees.story:
The seed was picked on New Year's Day, 1849, at Maryborough in Queensland, by John Carne Bidwill, the first director of the Royal Botanic Garden Sydney. It went into the Palm Grove in 1853 and the tree that came up is still standing there, more than 170 years later, pushing well clear of the palm canopy around it as one of the tallest things in the garden.

It is the Garden's type specimen of Queensland kauri, the first of the species planted here, and other kauris in Sydney get measured against it. A 2015 heritage survey of the Domain does exactly that: a companion kauri on Central Avenue, 31 metres tall with a canopy 16 metres across, is described as approaching the size of the 1853 tree in the Palm Grove. It has not caught up.

Kauris are slow and can run past 300 years, so at 170 this one is barely middle-aged. What it has instead is priority.

Nobody has published a trunk measurement for it, so if you get a tape around it we would like the figure. And our pin marks a point in the Palm Grove rather than the trunk itself, so allow a minute of standing among the palms and looking up. You are looking for the one that overtops the palms.

trees.name: The Quad Jacaranda
trees.age_estimate: not documented; the current tree is a 2017 clone, the site has carried a jacaranda since 1928

location.address: Main Quadrangle (south-eastern corner), University of Sydney, Camperdown NSW 2006

trees.access: Free; university campus grounds, the Quadrangle is generally open to visitors during daylight/campus hours
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Redfern station, or bus along City Road/Parramatta Road
trees.story:
The jacaranda in the Quadrangle is about nine years old. Say that first, because everything written about this tree is really about a different one: the jacaranda planted in the south-eastern corner in 1928 by Associate Professor Eben Gowrie Waterhouse, which toppled on 28 October 2016 after a root fungus ended 88 years of it. The BBC reported the death.

What stands there now was planted on 20 July 2017 and is a genetic clone of the tree that fell, propagated so the replacement would be the same jacaranda rather than merely another one. That is worth being clear about. You are not looking at a tree from 1928. You are looking at its cutting, growing into the same corner of the same sandstone quadrangle, with a flame tree put in beside it as a companion the same year.

The folklore transferred intact. Generations of Sydney students have held that if you have not started studying by the time the jacaranda flowers, you will fail your exams, which is a superstition that survives because the timing is genuinely cruel. The purple arrives in late October, just as the semester runs out.

The Quadrangle is open to visitors through daylight hours and the tree is easy to find. In flower it draws a crowd with phones. Out of flower it is a young tree with a great deal expected of it.

best_time.label: late October and November, when the Quadrangle turns purple

trees.name: The Port Jackson Fig of Vaucluse House

location.address: Vaucluse House, Wentworth Road, Vaucluse NSW 2030 (eastern side of the house, pleasure garden)

verified_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaucluse_House (cites the NSW State Heritage Register listing, SHR #955, via Smith 2014 and Stuart Read pers. comm. 2009)
trees.access: Free; the pleasure garden at Vaucluse House is open to the public Wednesday to Sunday, 10am-4pm, no charge (only the house interior is ticketed)
trees.transport: Bus 325 from Town Hall Station (Stand A, York Street) stops outside the gates; or T4 train to Edgecliff Station then transfer to the 325
trees.story:
Two records date this fig and they land a few years apart. Museums of History NSW puts the giant Port Jackson fig at the eastern corner of Vaucluse House in the mid-1850s. The State Heritage Register listing for the property calls it a Port Jackson fig of about 1859. Neither is a planting receipt, so the honest answer is that it went in somewhere inside that window, roughly 170 years ago, and nobody has narrowed it since.

It was planted as part of a fashion. Sydney's villa gardens were being laid out in the Thomas Shepherd manner, with specimen trees placed for effect on lawns meant to be walked across, and this fig is one of the survivors of that generation of planting. The Port Jackson fig is the local species rather than the imported showpiece, and it grows into exactly the wide, dark, low-branching shape those gardens were designed around. A century and a half on, it is doing what it was placed there to do.

Be careful which fig you are told about. A separate Moreton Bay fig stood between the house and the tea rooms until 1996, when it was removed and replaced by a cutting. Different tree, other side of the house.

The pleasure garden is free and open Wednesday to Sunday, ten until four, with only the house interior ticketed. Our pin is good to the eastern side of the house rather than to the trunk.

trees.name: The Vailele Moreton Bay Fig

location.address: Gale Street verge, Woolwich NSW 2110, adjacent to the side entrance of 2 The Point Road ('Vailele')

trees.access: Free; public street tree on the road verge, viewable and reachable at any time from the public footpath (no permission or ticket needed, this is council land not the private garden of Vailele next door)
trees.transport: Sydney Ferries F3 route from Circular Quay to Woolwich Wharf, about 23 minutes, then a short walk along the foreshore to Gale Street
trees.story:
This fig was dated by photograph. Hunter's Hill Council's tree register found what appears to be a small fig near this spot in pictures from about 1913, then a full-grown specimen in 1943 aerial survey imagery, and concluded that it would support a planting date of around 1900. That is one council reading two photographs, and it is the only source we have found on this tree at all, so treat the age as a reasonable inference rather than a record. If somebody has a better one, we want it.

The rest of the assessment is easier to check by standing in front of it. Seventeen metres tall, a canopy eighteen metres across, and a health rating that calls it an excellent example of the species. It grows on the Gale Street verge in Woolwich, on council land beside the side entrance of Vailele, a sandstone Federation house of about 1892; the register describes the tree as an important remnant planting associated with the house. The verge is public, so this one can be reached from the footpath at any hour.

Most people will see it from the water first. The register notes how visible it is from the Lane Cove River, and the best way here is the F3 ferry from Circular Quay to Woolwich Wharf, twenty-three minutes, then a walk up from the foreshore.

Do not confuse it with the two forest red gums further along the same street.

trees.name: The Camperdown Cemetery Fig

location.address: Camperdown Cemetery, near the Cemetery Lodge, 189 Church Street, Newtown NSW 2042

verified_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camperdown_Cemetery (citing Rees, T.G., 'Historic Camperdown', 1962; David Beaver, 'Camperdown Cemetery Draft Landscape Management Plan', Musescape, 1997; and Philippa Street, 'Camperdown Cemetery Tree Survey')
trees.access: Free; Camperdown Cemetery is a public heritage cemetery and park, gates generally open daylight hours
trees.transport: About 15-20 minutes on foot from Newtown or Stanmore stations, or a short bus ride from the Sydney CBD (roughly 4km away)
trees.story:
The canopy spans more than thirty metres, in a walled cemetery of four acres. It shades a good share of the dead.

The tree went in in 1848, the same year the cemetery itself opened, and the date is carried by a 1962 local history of Camperdown, a 1997 landscape management plan and the cemetery's own tree survey, with a 2010 account written from a site visit giving the same year independently. The reason given for the planting is softer. It is believed to have marked the roofing of the Cemetery Lodge, which the sources report as tradition rather than record, so take the ceremony loosely and the date firmly.

With the oaks put in the same year, it is the oldest tree in the Marrickville district. Camperdown is the oldest surviving cemetery in Sydney, the walled remnant of a much larger burial ground that Newtown grew around, and the fig stands near the Lodge by the Church Street entrance, so it is the first thing you meet coming through the gate.

Nobody has published a trunk measurement, which for a fig of 178 years is a gap worth closing. If you tape it, send us the number.

The cemetery is free and open through daylight hours, fifteen to twenty minutes on foot from Newtown or Stanmore stations. Our pin sits on the cemetery rather than the tree, though at that size it will not cost you long.

trees.name: The Wishing Tree

location.address: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney, Mrs Macquaries Road, Sydney NSW 2000 (towards the Harbour side of the Garden)

verified_sources: https://mirrorsydney.wordpress.com/2013/03/21/sydney-trees/ (Vanessa Berry, local history blog, fetched directly)
trees.access: Free; Royal Botanic Garden Sydney, open daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Martin Place or St James stations, same cluster as the Bidwill Kauri Pine (syd_001)
trees.notes: Pin: OpenStreetMap carries a node explicitly named Wishing Tree at this point, on the harbour side of the Garden. It replaces the Garden-centre coordinate the first pass used. One crowd-maintained source, so the precision stays approximate until somebody standing there tells us otherwise.
trees.story:
A plaque on the trunk explains that this tree will never reach the grandeur of the one it replaced, because a storm damaged its crown soon after it was planted. It is an unusually honest thing for a label to say, and it is accurate.

The original Wishing Tree was a Norfolk Island pine set out from a tub around 1816, under Elizabeth Macquarie's eye. By 1905 it was over thirty metres and the most popular tree in the Royal Botanic Garden, with a custom attached: three times around it forwards, three times backwards, and then make your wish. In the 1930s it was found to be dying of old age, and a replacement was bought with money raised by the Farmer's Children's Radio Birthday Club and planted nearby. The original came down in 1945 and its timber was turned into souvenirs, sold to raise funds for returned servicemen.

So the tree you will stand in front of, on the harbour side of the garden, is that 1930s replacement. Roughly ninety years old, shortened by one storm early in its life, and still being walked around: visitors were doing their six laps in 2018.

Two notes. The spot where the original stood now holds a Wollemi pine, a different tree with a different story. And our pin follows a map node named for the Wishing Tree rather than a surveyed position, so leave room for a short hunt.
